name: Ensoniq EPS-16 Plus
originalPurpose: A keyboard sampling workstation: sixteen-bit sampling, filters, effects and an eight-track sequencer, sold to musicians as a more affordable alternative to studio samplers.
whatActuallyHappened: RZA traded in his SP-1200 for one and used it to build the long, melancholy loops of Wu-Tang Clan's first album, including 'C.R.E.A.M.'. He later sold it to the Wu-affiliated producer True Master, who made more Wu records on it. Ensoniq's cheaper samplers put the whole-phrase loop within reach of producers without a studio budget.
priceStory: It launched at 1,795 pounds in the UK. No US launch price is sourced here. Ensoniq's selling point from the Mirage onward was a lower price than the big studio samplers, which is how its machines reached home producers.
hook: The keyboard sampler RZA used to build Wu-Tang's first album, after he traded his SP-1200 for it.
blurb: The EPS-16 Plus was a keyboard that could record short pieces of sound and loop them. It had more memory and a cleaner sound than the SP-1200, and it marks a shift from short, gritty fragments to longer, cleaner loops of whole phrases. RZA of the Wu-Tang Clan swapped his SP-1200 for one, the clearest single example of that shift, and started making loops two and four bars long instead of single hits. The sad piano on 'C.R.E.A.M.' came out of this machine. The end year here is when its successor, the ASR-10, arrived in 1992. That stands in for the end of production rather than being a documented date, as with the Simmons SDS-V (A111).
